claim: C. elegans memo-1 (C37C3.8) shares 153 out of 297 amino acids (52%) identity with human Memo1.
source: The nematode C. elegans encodes a gene (C37C3.8) that shares 153 out of 297 amino acids (52%) identity with human Memo1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), which we named memo-1 (Mediator of ErbB2-driven cell motility-like protein; wormbase.org).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and stated in the text.

claim: memo-1 is expressed in the embryo and larval stages and through adulthood in many neuronal and non-neuronal cells in C. elegans.
source: The C. elegans memo-1 gene product is expressed in the embryo and larval stages and through adulthood in many neuronal and non-neuronal cells in the head and tail, spermatheca, distal tip cells, anchor cell, and intestine (jxEx8 [Pmemo-1::GFP] and ldEx112 [MEMOfosmid::GFP]; Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–I).
evidence: Expression pattern is demonstrated through transgenic GFP reporter constructs shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–I.

claim: memo-1(RNAi) increases lifespan by 7–38% compared to wild type.
source: Both memo-1(RNAi)) and memo-1(gk345) mutants showed a 7–38% increase in lifespan compared to wild type (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data from multiple experiments shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: memo-1(gk345) mutants show a 27% increase in mean lifespan compared to wild type at 20°C.
source: memo-1(gk345) mutants show a 27% increase in mean lifespan compared to wild type (N2) at 20°C. P value determined by log-rank. Statistics and additional lifespan data are in Supplementary file 1.
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: Adult-specific knockdown of memo-1 is sufficient to increase lifespan.
source: To exclude any developmental effects of memo-1 loss, we treated wild-type animals with memo-1(RNAi) starting from the first day of adulthood and showed that this was sufficient to increase lifespan (Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data from adult-specific RNAi treatment shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Knockdown of memo-1 starting on the first day of adulthood increases mean lifespan by 20% compared to empty RNAi vector control at 20°C.
source: Knockdown of memo-1(RNAi#1) starting on the first day of adulthood in RNAi-sensitive animals (rrf-3(pk1426)) increases mean lifespan by 20% compared to empty RNAi vector control (L4440) at 20°C. P value determined by log-rank. Statistics and additional lifespan data are in Supplementary file 1.
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: memo-1(RNAi) treated wild type animals have higher mRNA expression levels of oxidative stress response genes compared to empty vector treated wild type.
source: memo-1(RNAi#2) treated wild type (N2) (-) have higher mRNA expression levels of the oxidative stress response genes, such as glutamine cysteine synthetase (gcs-1), glutathione-S-transferase (gst-1, 4, 5, 38), and uridine 5'-diphospho-glucuronosyltransferase (ugt-8, 25, 58), compared to empty vector treated wild type (N2) (+), determined by qRT-PCR. 3 replicates of >1000 mixed staged worms per condition were analysed. Data are represented as mean ± s.e.m. P value * <0.05, ** <0.001, *** <0.0001 relative to wild type or control, by one sample t-test, two-tailed, hypothetical mean of 1.
evidence: qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E with statistical analysis.

claim: Loss of memo-1 increases the expression of oxidative stress response genes gst-4 and gcs-1 in the intestine.
source: Loss of memo-1 increases the expression of oxidative stress response genes gst-4 and gcs-1 in the intestine. (F) shows representative pictures of dvIs19 [Pgst-4::GFP] transgenic adult C. elegans treated with empty vector (upper picture; category: none) or memo-1(RNAi#1) (lower picture; category: high). Anterior to the right, ventral side up. Scale bar = 100 µm. (G–I) Quantification of transgenic worms containing the promoter of gst-4 or gcs-1 fused with GFP (dvIs19 [Pgst-4::GFP] and ldIs003 [Pgcs-1::GFP]. Scoring is described in Material and methods. Three trials are shown with N > 60 for each condition and trial. P value by chi2 (* <0.05; ** <0.001; ***p<0.0001).
evidence: GFP reporter expression data shown in Figure 1F–I with quantification and statistical analysis.

claim: memo-1(gk345) mutants show increased survival in sodium arsenite (5 mM) compared to wild type.
source: Survival of one-day old adult memo-1(gk345) mutants or wild type (N2) in sodium arsenite (5 mM) was assayed. P value determined by log-rank. Statistics and additional oxidative stress data either with arsenite or tert-butyl hydrogen peroxide are shown in Supplementary file 2.
evidence: Oxidative stress survival data shown in Figure 1J with statistical analysis.

claim: memo-1(-) mutants have normal pharyngeal pumping rates similar to wild type.
source: Since MEMO-1 is expressed around the pharynx (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), an organ that regulates food intake, we measured pharyngeal pumping rates of memo-1(-) mutants, finding them to be similar to those of wild type (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Pharyngeal pumping data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: memo-1(-) mutants have normal brood size.
source: However, memo-1(-) mutants did not show germ-line defects (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G). Not only did they have a normal brood size (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), they also showed no upregulation of genes implicated in reduced germline stem cell-mediated longevity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Brood size data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: memo-1(-) mutants do not show upregulation of genes involved in the heat shock response, the unfolded protein response (UPR) and other longevity-promoting processes.
source: By contrast, genes involved in the heat shock response, the unfolded protein response (UPR) and other longevity-promoting processes were not altered in memo-1(-) animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and E).
evidence: Gene expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and E.

claim: Downregulation or loss of memo-1 by RNAi or mutation increases oxidative stress resistance.
source: Importantly, downregulation or loss of memo-1 by RNAi or mutation increased oxidative stress resistance, correlating with the observed changes in gene expression (Figure 1J, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Oxidative stress resistance data shown in Figure 1J and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Loss of memo-1 does not increase resistance to heat shock.
source: By contrast, its loss did not increase resistance to heat shock (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: Heat shock resistance data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3H.

claim: Elevated oxidative stress resistance is an important factor in memo-1(-)-longevity.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that a elevated oxidative stress resistance might be an important factor in memo-1(-)-longevity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between increased oxidative stress resistance and longevity in memo-1(-) animals.

claim: Several oxidative stress response genes upregulated in memo-1 mutants are direct transcriptional targets of SKN-1.
source: Several of the oxidative stress response genes that are upregulated by memo-1 knockdown or mutation are direct transcriptional targets of SKN-1 (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Target gene information provided in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Knockdown of skn-1 by RNAi abolishes the longevity phenotype of memo-1(-) mutants.
source: Knockdown of skn-1 by RNAi abolished the longevity phenotype of memo-1(-) mutants (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: memo-1(RNAi) knockdown increases lifespan of wild-type animals but not of skn-1(-) mutants.
source: Conversely, memo-1(RNAi) knockdown increased lifespan of wild-type animals but not of skn-1(-) mutants (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The extended lifespan of animals that lack memo-1 is mediated through SKN-1.
source: These results suggest that the extended lifespan of animals that lack memo-1 is mediated through SKN-1.
evidence: This conclusion is based on genetic epistasis experiments showing skn-1 is required for memo-1(-) longevity.

claim: RNAi-mediated memo-1 knockdown causes a significant increase in nuclear SKN-1::GFP.
source: RNAi-mediated memo-1 knockdown caused a significant increase in nuclear SKN-1::GFP (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: SKN-1::GFP localization data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Reducing memo-1 function either by RNAi or mutation results in higher levels of phospho-p38 MAPK.
source: Importantly, reducing memo-1 function either by RNAi or mutation resulted in higher levels of phospho-p38 MAPK (Figure 2E and F), and loss of sek-1 completely abolished memo-1(-) mediated-longevity (Figure 2G).
evidence: Western blot data for phospho-p38 MAPK shown in Figure 2E and F, and lifespan data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Loss of sek-1 completely abolishes memo-1(-) mediated-longevity.
source: Importantly, reducing memo-1 function either by RNAi or mutation resulted in higher levels of phospho-p38 MAPK (Figure 2E and F), and loss of sek-1 completely abolished memo-1(-) mediated-longevity (Figure 2G).
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: memo-1 mutants remain long-lived compared to wild type on heat-killed bacteria.
source: Since sek-1 and skn-1 are important for the defense against pathogenic bacteria (Hoeven et al., 2011), and bacterial proliferation in the C. elegans' intestine contributes to death of the animal (Garigan et al., 2002), we investigated the lifespan of memo-1 mutants on heat-killed bacteria. We found that memo-1 mutants remain long-lived compared to wild type (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data on heat-killed bacteria provided in Supplementary file 1.

claim: memo-1 loss stimulates the p38 MAPK oxidative stress response pathway, which is required for the longevity phenotype.
source: Taken together, these results show that memo-1 loss stimulates the p38 MAPK oxidative stress response pathway (Figure 2H), which is required for the longevity phenotype.
evidence: This conclusion is based on genetic and biochemical data showing p38 MAPK activation and requirement for longevity.

claim: Treatment of wild-type C. elegans with memo-1(RNAi) results in a 2-fold increase in intracellular ROS measured by CM-H2DCFDA.
source: To examine this, we measured intracellular ROS in living worms using a diffusible fluorescent probe (chloromethyl derivative CM-H2DCFDA) and observed a 2-fold increase upon treatment of wild-type C. elegans with memo-1(RNAi) (Figure 3A).
evidence: ROS measurement data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Transgenic worms expressing the HyPer sensor treated with memo-1(RNAi) have a 5-fold increase in endogenous hydrogen peroxide levels.
source: Moreover, compared to control worms, transgenic worms that express the HyPer sensor (jrIs1 [Back et al., 2012b]) and have been treated with memo-1(RNAi) have a 5-fold increase in endogenous hydrogen peroxide levels (Figure 3B), while memo-1 mutant or RNAi-treated animals have a 2-fold increase in hydrogen peroxide, according to the fluorescent probe AmplexRed (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Hydrogen peroxide measurement data shown in Figure 3B using HyPer sensor.

claim: memo-1 mutant or RNAi-treated animals have a 2-fold increase in hydrogen peroxide according to the fluorescent probe AmplexRed.
source: Moreover, compared to control worms, transgenic worms that express the HyPer sensor (jrIs1 [Back et al., 2012b]) and have been treated with memo-1(RNAi) have a 5-fold increase in endogenous hydrogen peroxide levels (Figure 3B), while memo-1 mutant or RNAi-treated animals have a 2-fold increase in hydrogen peroxide, according to the fluorescent probe AmplexRed (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Hydrogen peroxide measurement data shown in Figure 3C and D using AmplexRed.

claim: ROS levels in memo-1(RNAi) and memo-1(RNAi); sek-1(RNAi) animals are elevated to a similar level.
source: Interestingly, ROS levels in the memo-1(RNAi) and the memo-1(RNAi); sek-1(RNAi) animals were elevated to a similar level (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that the SKN-1 adaptive response did not necessarily reduce the overall ROS load.
evidence: ROS measurement data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The SKN-1 adaptive response does not necessarily reduce the overall ROS load in memo-1(-) animals.
source: Interestingly, ROS levels in the memo-1(RNAi) and the memo-1(RNAi); sek-1(RNAi) animals were elevated to a similar level (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that the SKN-1 adaptive response did not necessarily reduce the overall ROS load.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ROS levels remain elevated even when the SKN-1 pathway is blocked.

claim: memo-1(-)-impaired animals that lack ROS protection in a skn-1(-) or sek-1(-) mutant background do not live shorter than either skn-1(-) or sek-1(-) single mutants.
source: Additionally, memo-1(-)-impaired animals that lack ROS protection in a skn-1(-) (Figure 2B) or sek-1(-) mutant background (Figure 2G) did not live shorter than either skn-1(-) or sek-1(-) single mutants in the absence (Figure 2B and G) or presence of the oxidative stress-inducing agent 5 mM arsenite (Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 2B and G, and Supplementary files 1 and 2.

claim: The increased ROS levels in animals that lack memo-1 are not necessarily detrimental.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the increased ROS levels in animals that lack memo-1 are not necessarily detrimental.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that elevated ROS in memo-1(-) animals do not cause additional harm in the absence of protective responses.

claim: GSH treatment abolishes memo-1(-)-induced longevity.
source: GSH treatment during adulthood had no effect on wild-type lifespan, but abolished memo-1(-)-induced longevity (Figure 3H, Supplementary file 1), suggesting an essential role for memo-1(-)-induced ROS in this process.
evidence: Lifespan data with GSH treatment shown in Figure 3H and Supplementary file 1.

claim: memo-1(-)-induced ROS are essential for the longevity phenotype.
source: GSH treatment during adulthood had no effect on wild-type lifespan, but abolished memo-1(-)-induced longevity (Figure 3H, Supplementary file 1), suggesting an essential role for memo-1(-)-induced ROS in this process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neutralizing ROS with GSH eliminates the longevity benefit.

claim: GSH treatment abolishes the induction of the SKN-1 target gene gst-4 by memo-1(RNAi).
source: Furthermore, GSH treatment abolished the induction of the SKN-1 target gene gst-4 (Figure 3I), indicating that the memo-1(RNAi)-induced ROS are responsible for SKN-1 activation.
evidence: GFP reporter expression data with GSH treatment shown in Figure 3I.

claim: memo-1(RNAi)-induced ROS are responsible for SKN-1 activation.
source: Furthermore, GSH treatment abolished the induction of the SKN-1 target gene gst-4 (Figure 3I), indicating that the memo-1(RNAi)-induced ROS are responsible for SKN-1 activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neutralizing ROS prevents SKN-1 target gene induction.

claim: memo-1(RNAi) animals have similar mitochondrial ROS levels as controls measured with MitoTracker Red CM-H2X.
source: To determine if excess ROS in memo-1(-) mutants are generated from mitochondria, we used a specific mitochondrial ROS-detecting reagent, MitoTracker Red CM-H2X (Weimer et al., 2014), revealing that the memo-1(RNAi) animals had similar mitochondrial ROS levels as the controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: Mitochondrial ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The mitochondria-specific antioxidant MitoTEMPO does not suppress the higher ROS levels in memo-1(RNAi)-treated animals.
source: Furthermore, a mitochondria specific-antioxidant, MitoTEMPO, neither suppressed the higher ROS levels nor elevated the gst-4 expression levels (Figure 4C) seen in memo-1(RNAi)-treated animals (Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: ROS measurement and GFP reporter data with MitoTEMPO treatment shown in Figure 4B, 4C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The level of hsp-6 expression remains at control levels in memo-1(RNAi) animals.
source: The level of hsp-6 expression, a measure of the mitochondrial unfolded protein response and of high mitochondrial ROS levels (Runkel et al., 2013), remained at control levels in memo-1(RNAi) animals (Figure 4D).
evidence: hsp-6 expression data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The longevity of memo-1(RNAi) treated animals is additive to the longevity of electron transport chain mitochondrial mutant isp-1(qm150).
source: Moreover, the longevity of memo-1(RNAi) treated animals was additive to the longevity of electron transport chain mitochondrial mutant isp-1(qm150) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data provided in Supplementary file 1.

claim: memo-1(-) longevity is independent of sod-3.
source: Lastly and importantly, a low dose of mitochondrial ROS require sod-3 (superoxide dismutase) for extending lifespan (Yee et al., 2014) and memo-1(-) longevity is independent of sod-3 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data provided in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The memo-1(-) induced ROS are not generated by the mitochondria.
source: Taken together, these data show that the memo-1(-) induced ROS are not generated by the mitochondria.
evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of evidence showing no increase in mitochondrial ROS and independence from mitochondrial pathways.

claim: DPI treatment completely eliminates memo-1(RNAi)-induced ROS.
source: To check if they have a role in ROS production in memo-1(RNAi)-animals, we treated these animals with diphenyleneiodonium (DPI), a general inhibitor of NADPH oxidase activity (Stuehr et al., 1991). DPI treatment completely eliminated memo-1(RNAi)-induced ROS (Figure 4E).
evidence: ROS measurement data with DPI treatment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: BLI-3 is mainly expressed and functional in the intestine and hypodermis of adult C. elegans.
source: The C. elegans genome encodes two NADPH oxidase (NOX)-related genes, Duox1/BLI-3 and Duox2. NOX proteins contain an NADPH oxidase domain, while DUOX proteins possess an additional peroxidase domain. Duox2 is not expressed in adult C. elegans, while BLI-3 is mainly expressed and functional in the intestine and hypodermis (Edens et al., 2001; Chávez et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Edens et al., 2001; Chávez et al., 2009).

claim: Knocking down bli-3 completely eliminates memo-1(-)-induced ROS.
source: Importantly, knocking down bli-3 completely eliminated memo-1(-)-induced ROS (Figure 4F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that this dual oxidase is required for ROS generation in the memo-1(-) animals.
evidence: ROS measurement data with bli-3 knockdown shown in Figure 4F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: BLI-3 dual oxidase is required for ROS generation in memo-1(-) animals.
source: Importantly, knocking down bli-3 completely eliminated memo-1(-)-induced ROS (Figure 4F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that this dual oxidase is required for ROS generation in the memo-1(-) animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bli-3 knockdown eliminates ROS in memo-1(-) animals.

claim: Adult-specific knockdown of bli-3 does not alter wild-type lifespan.
source: Adult-specific knockdown of bli-3 did not alter wild-type lifespan or longevity resulting from dietary restriction, reduced insulin/IGF-1 signaling or reduced mitochondrial electron transport chain activity (Supplementary file 1), but it completely eliminated the memo-1(-) longevity phenotype (Figure 4G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data provided in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Adult-specific knockdown of bli-3 completely eliminates the memo-1(-) longevity phenotype.
source: Adult-specific knockdown of bli-3 did not alter wild-type lifespan or longevity resulting from dietary restriction, reduced insulin/IGF-1 signaling or reduced mitochondrial electron transport chain activity (Supplementary file 1), but it completely eliminated the memo-1(-) longevity phenotype (Figure 4G and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 4G and Supplementary file 1.

claim: bli-3 knockdown suppresses SKN-1 nuclear localization in memo-1(RNAi) animals.
source: Consistent with this, bli-3 knockdown suppressed SKN-1 nuclear localization in memo-1(RNAi) animals (Figure 4H), suggesting that BLI-3-generated ROS signal to SKN-1.
evidence: SKN-1::GFP localization data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: BLI-3-generated ROS signal to SKN-1.
source: Consistent with this, bli-3 knockdown suppressed SKN-1 nuclear localization in memo-1(RNAi) animals (Figure 4H), suggesting that BLI-3-generated ROS signal to SKN-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that blocking BLI-3 prevents SKN-1 activation.

claim: Overexpression of BLI-3 alone, or with its maturation/association partners DOXA-1 and TSP-15, is sufficient to generate higher ROS levels.
source: Conversely, overexpression of BLI-3 alone, or with its maturation/association partners DOXA-1 and TSP-15 (Moribe et al., 2012), was sufficient to generate higher ROS levels (Figure 4I) and to increase lifespan (Figure 4J and Supplementary file 1), which was reduced by bli-3 (RNAi) (Figure 4K and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Overexpression of BLI-3 is sufficient to increase lifespan.
source: Conversely, overexpression of BLI-3 alone, or with its maturation/association partners DOXA-1 and TSP-15 (Moribe et al., 2012), was sufficient to generate higher ROS levels (Figure 4I) and to increase lifespan (Figure 4J and Supplementary file 1), which was reduced by bli-3 (RNAi) (Figure 4K and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 4J and Supplementary file 1.

claim: BLI-3-dependent longevity requires SKN-1.
source: BLI-3-dependent longevity (Figure 4J and Supplementary file 1) required SKN-1 (Figure 4L and Supplementary file 1), and was suppressed by the antioxidant GSH (Figure 4M and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 4L and Supplementary file 1.

claim: BLI-3-dependent longevity is suppressed by the antioxidant GSH.
source: BLI-3-dependent longevity (Figure 4J and Supplementary file 1) required SKN-1 (Figure 4L and Supplementary file 1), and was suppressed by the antioxidant GSH (Figure 4M and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 4M and Supplementary file 1.

claim: MEMO-1 functions as an inhibitor of BLI-3.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that MEMO-1 functions as an inhibitor of BLI-3; and elevated ROS in the absence of MEMO-1 confers an enhanced longevity phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of MEMO-1 increases BLI-3 activity and ROS production.

claim: Elevated ROS in the absence of MEMO-1 confers an enhanced longevity phenotype.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that MEMO-1 functions as an inhibitor of BLI-3; and elevated ROS in the absence of MEMO-1 confers an enhanced longevity phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of increased ROS and longevity in memo-1(-) animals.

claim: BLI-3 produces ROS for innate immune functions.
source: This is a novel function for the NADPH oxidase BLI-3, which is known to produce ROS for innate immune functions (Chávez et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Chávez et al., 2009).

claim: Loss of memo-1 increases expression of the SKN-1-target gene gst-4 in a bli-3-dependent manner.
source: Loss of memo-1 increases expression of the SKN-1-target gene gst-4 in a bli-3-dependent manner (Figure 5A).
evidence: GFP reporter expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Reduction of insulin/IGF-1 receptor signaling by daf-2(RNAi) induces gst-4 via SKN-1 and is not blocked by bli-3(RNAi).
source: By contrast, reduction of insulin/IGF-1 receptor signaling by daf-2(RNAi), which induces gst-4 via SKN-1 (Ewald et al., 2015; Tullet et al., 2008), was not blocked by bli-3(RNAi) (Figure 5A bars 5–7).
evidence: GFP reporter expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MEMO-1 and DAF-2 act in parallel to each other.
source: These findings would suggest that MEMO-1 and DAF-2 act in parallel to each other.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bli-3 is required for memo-1 effects but not for daf-2 effects on gst-4 expression.

claim: A targeted RNAi screen identified known activators of mammalian NADPH oxidases as required for memo-1(-) induced gst-4 expression.
source: In this screen, we identified known activators of mammalian NADPH oxidases, such as rac-2, a Rho family GTPase, pak-1, the p21-activated kinase (Stanley et al., 2014; Hurd et al., 2012), doxa-1, the C. elegans BLI-3 maturation factor (Moribe et al., 2012), pes-7/IQGAP, the actin-binding Rho GTPase activator and NRF2 binding partner (Kim et al., 2013), and two interactors of mammalian Memo1: the actin-binding depolymerizing factor unc-60/cofilin (Meira et al., 2009) and the homologue of the mammalian RhoA GTPase rho-1 (Stanley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on the RNAi screen results and cited literature.

claim: Knocking down rho-1 in memo-1(RNAi) animals results in complete elimination of their oxidative stress resistance.
source: To test whether C. elegans rho-1 is required for memo-1(-)-induced oxidative stress resistance, we knocked-down rho-1 in memo-1(RNAi) animals, which resulted in complete elimination of their oxidative stress resistance (Figure 5B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Oxidative stress resistance data shown in Figure 5B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Knocking down rho-1 in memo-1(gk345) mutants partially suppresses the memo-1(-) ROS induction.
source: Knocking down rho-1 in memo-1(gk345) mutants partially suppressed the memo-1(-) ROS induction (Figure 5C).
evidence: ROS measurement data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Adult-specific knockdown of rho-1 completely suppresses the longevity of memo-1(gk345).
source: Moreover, adult-specific knockdown of rho-1 completely suppressed the longevity of memo-1(gk345), and partially blocked the lifespan extension from BLI-3 overexpression (Figure 5D and E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 5D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Adult-specific knockdown of rho-1 partially blocks the lifespan extension from BLI-3 overexpression.
source: Moreover, adult-specific knockdown of rho-1 completely suppressed the longevity of memo-1(gk345), and partially blocked the lifespan extension from BLI-3 overexpression (Figure 5D and E and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Lifespan data shown in Figure 5E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: MEMO-1 and RHO-1 physically interact in C. elegans lysates under normal conditions.
source: Next, we examined whether MEMO-1 and RHO-1 physically interact in C. elegans lysates, by performing co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) of endogenous RHO-1 followed by immunoblot analysis of GFP-tagged MEMO-1. Under normal conditions, MEMO-1 and RHO-1 are found in a complex (Figure 5F).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Under normal conditions endogenous RHO-1 physically binds to endogenous BLI-3 in vivo.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation with a RHO-1 antibody revealed that under normal conditions endogenous RHO-1 physically binds to endogenous BLI-3 in vivo. However, we found 2.25-fold higher levels of the BLI-3 bound to RHO-1 in lysates from memo-1 knockdown worms (Figure 5G).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: There are 2.25-fold higher levels of BLI-3 bound to RHO-1 in lysates from memo-1 knockdown worms.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation with a RHO-1 antibody revealed that under normal conditions endogenous RHO-1 physically binds to endogenous BLI-3 in vivo. However, we found 2.25-fold higher levels of the BLI-3 bound to RHO-1 in lysates from memo-1 knockdown worms (Figure 5G).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: MEMO-1 regulates the RHO-1/BLI-3 interactions necessary for BLI-3 function.
source: These findings suggest that MEMO-1 regulates the RHO-1/BLI-3 interactions necessary for BLI-3 function, a model that is consistent with our genetic findings.
evidence: This is inferred from the biochemical and genetic data showing MEMO-1 affects RHO-1/BLI-3 interaction.

claim: The memo-1 promoter contains four predicted SKN-1 binding sites.
source: Interestingly, the memo-1 promoter contains four predicted SKN-1 binding sites (wormbase.org).
evidence: This is stated based on information from wormbase.org.

claim: Transgenic SKN-1::GFP shows a high signal on two of the four sites in the memo-1 promoter region in a genome-wide screen.
source: In a genome-wide screen, transgenic SKN-1::GFP showed a high signal on two of the four sites in the memo-1 promoter region (Figure 5H, upper panel; [Niu et al., 2011]), suggesting that SKN-1 regulates memo-1 transcription.
evidence: ChIP data shown in Figure 5H upper panel from cited study (Niu et al., 2011).

claim: SKN-1 regulates memo-1 transcription.
source: In a genome-wide screen, transgenic SKN-1::GFP showed a high signal on two of the four sites in the memo-1 promoter region (Figure 5H, upper panel; [Niu et al., 2011]), suggesting that SKN-1 regulates memo-1 transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from SKN-1 binding to the memo-1 promoter and expression changes.

claim: memo-1 mRNA levels are lower in skn-1(zu67) loss-of-function mutants.
source: Consistent with this, memo-1 mRNA levels are lower in skn-1(zu67) loss-of-function mutants and, conversely, higher in transgenic animals with either SKN-1 overexpression (ldIs007 [SKN-1::GFP]), or constitutive nuclear SKN-1 overexpression (ldIs020 [SKN-1S393::GFP]; [Tullet et al., 2008]), when compared to wild type.
evidence: qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5H lower panel.

claim: memo-1 mRNA levels are higher in transgenic animals with SKN-1 overexpression or constitutive nuclear SKN-1 overexpression.
source: Consistent with this, memo-1 mRNA levels are lower in skn-1(zu67) loss-of-function mutants and, conversely, higher in transgenic animals with either SKN-1 overexpression (ldIs007 [SKN-1::GFP]), or constitutive nuclear SKN-1 overexpression (ldIs020 [SKN-1S393::GFP]; [Tullet et al., 2008]), when compared to wild type.
evidence: qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5H lower panel.

claim: MEMO-1 controls the level of RHO-1 that is bound to BLI-3, and thereby regulates BLI-3 activity.
source: These results suggest a model whereby MEMO-1 controls the level of RHO-1 that is bound to BLI-3, and thereby regulates BLI-3 activity (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a model inferred from the combined biochemical and genetic data.

claim: In animals with memo-1 knockdown, RHO-1 is free to bind and activate BLI-3/NADPH oxidase, thereby generating an increase in intracellular ROS.
source: In animals with memo-1 knockdown RHO-1 is free to bind and activate BLI-3/NADPH oxidase, thereby generating an increase in intracellular ROS.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from the data showing increased RHO-1/BLI-3 interaction and ROS in memo-1(-) animals.

claim: ROS generated by BLI-3 act as a longevity-promoting signal molecule that activates both p38 MAPK and the SKN-1/Nrf1,2,3 transcription factor.
source: These ROS presumably act as a longevity-promoting signal molecule that activates both p38 MAPK and the SKN-1/Nrf1,2,3 transcription factor, which would increase the level of transcripts involved in the oxidative stress response, thus lengthening lifespan.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from the combined data on ROS, p38 MAPK, SKN-1, and longevity.

claim: Activation of SKN-1 increases the expression of memo-1, suggesting a negative feedback loop that regulates ROS generation by the BLI-3/NADPH oxidase.
source: Furthermore, activation of SKN-1 increases the expression of memo-1 (Figure 5H), suggesting a negative feedback loop that regulates ROS generation by the BLI-3/NADPH oxidase (Figure 6) in order to maintain a homeostatic balance.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SKN-1 upregulates memo-1, which inhibits BLI-3.

claim: NADPH oxidases are a major source of cellular ROS.
source: NADPH oxidases are a major source of cellular ROS (Krause, 2007), but the possibility that the ROS they produce might influence longevity-associated mechanisms has not been explored.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Krause, 2007).

claim: MEMO-1 is a negative regulator of BLI-3.
source: We show that MEMO-1 is a negative regulator of BLI-3, and that its loss enhances an interaction between RHO-1 and BLI-3, thereby stimulating the activity of this NADPH oxidase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined biochemical and genetic data presented in the study.

claim: Loss of MEMO-1 enhances an interaction between RHO-1 and BLI-3, thereby stimulating the activity of this NADPH oxidase.
source: We show that MEMO-1 is a negative regulator of BLI-3, and that its loss enhances an interaction between RHO-1 and BLI-3, thereby stimulating the activity of this NADPH oxidase.
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation data showing increased RHO-1/BLI-3 interaction in memo-1(-) animals.

claim: ROS generated by BLI-3 activate p38 and induce nuclear accumulation of SKN-1/Nrf, and thereby promote stress resistance and longevity.
source: As a result, ROS are generated that activate p38 and induce nuclear accumulation of SKN-1/Nrf, and thereby promote stress resistance and longevity in this metazoan.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data showing ROS production, p38 activation, SKN-1 nuclear localization, and increased stress resistance and longevity.

claim: The data identify a regulatory mechanism that controls ROS generation, which is sufficient to promote longevity.
source: Thus, our data identify a regulatory mechanism that controls ROS generation, which is sufficient to promote longevity; they also show that this mechanism initiates an adaptive response similar to that triggered by transient ROS increases generated from the mitochondria.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data presented in the study.

claim: The MEMO-1/BLI-3 mechanism initiates an adaptive response similar to that triggered by transient ROS increases generated from the mitochondria.
source: Thus, our data identify a regulatory mechanism that controls ROS generation, which is sufficient to promote longevity; they also show that this mechanism initiates an adaptive response similar to that triggered by transient ROS increases generated from the mitochondria.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of the NADPH oxidase pathway with known mitochondrial ROS signaling pathways.

claim: Directed ROS generation acts as a homeostatic signal that can have substantial benefits.
source: Our findings support and broaden the emerging hypothesis that directed ROS generation, e.g., in response to specific stimuli or in particular subcellular locations, acts as a homeostatic signal that can have substantial benefits (Hekimi et al., 2011; Shadel, 2014; Ristow and Schmeisser, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion supported by the current findings and cited literature.

claim: The mitochondria generate ROS as a by-product of oxidative phosphorylation, and thereby integrate the rate of metabolism with the animal's physiology.
source: The mitochondria generate ROS as a by-product of oxidative phosphorylation, and thereby integrate the rate of metabolism with the animal's physiology.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mitochondrial ROS.

claim: The beneficial effects of low-dose mitochondrial ROS on healthspan and lifespan arise from a hormetic adaptation to mild stress.
source: The beneficial effects of low-dose mitochondrial ROS on healthspan and lifespan arise from a hormetic adaptation to mild stress (Hekimi et al., 2011; Shadel, 2014; Ristow and Schmeisser, 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: ROS production arising from perturbed ER redox homeostasis leads to a protective response that increases lifespan.
source: Similarly, it was shown recently that ROS production arising from perturbed ER redox homeostasis leads to a protective response that increases lifespan (Hourihan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Hourihan et al., 2016).

claim: Mutants that lack the capacity to detoxify ROS (e.g. skn-1(-) and sek-1(-)) exhibit a shortening of lifespan when mitochondrial or ER ROS are elevated.
source: In each of these examples, mutants that lack the capacity to detoxify ROS (e.g. skn-1(-) and sek-1(-)) exhibit a shortening of lifespan, indicating that these ROS are detrimental in the absence of this response (Schmeisser et al., 2013b; Weimer et al., 2014; Schmeisser et al., 2013a; Hunt et al., 2011; Saul et al., 2010; Hourihan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: ROS generated by the BLI-3 NADPH oxidase did not further shorten the lifespan of memo-1 mutant animals that lack the oxidative stress response genes skn-1 and sek-1.
source: By contrast, ROS generated by the BLI-3 NADPH oxidase did not further shorten the lifespan of memo-1 mutant animals that lack the oxidative stress response genes skn-1 and sek-1 (Figure 2A,B and G).
evidence: This is based on lifespan data shown in Figure 2A, B, and G.

claim: The health benefits from NADPH oxidase-generated ROS are initiated by a signaling cascade in the absence of an adaptive stress response to damage, and therefore arise from a ROS signal per se.
source: This suggests that the health benefits from NADPH oxidase-generated ROS are initiated by a signaling cascade in the absence of an adaptive stress response to damage, and therefore arise from a ROS signal per se.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that NADPH oxidase ROS do not cause additional harm in the absence of protective responses, unlike mitochondrial ROS.

claim: A variety of extracellular and intracellular stimuli induce NADPH oxidase activation.
source: A variety of extracellular and intracellular stimuli induce NADPH oxidase activation (Lambeth and Neish, 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Lambeth and Neish, 2014).

claim: In C. elegans the NADPH oxidase BLI-3 produces ROS in response to pathogen infection, leading to activation of NSY-1/ASK1/MAPKKK, SEK-1/MAPKK, PMK-1/p38 MAPK and SKN-1/Nrf.
source: The roles of these enzymes in innate immunity are well-documented, and in C. elegans the NADPH oxidase BLI-3 produces ROS in response to pathogen infection, leading in turn to activation of NSY-1/ASK1/MAPKKK, SEK-1/MAPKK, PMK-1/p38 MAPK and SKN-1/Nrf (Hoeven et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Hoeven et al., 2011).

claim: BLI-3 and p38/SKN-1 are activated by stress from sodium arsenite.
source: BLI-3 and p38/SKN-1 are also activated by stress from sodium arsenite (Hourihan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Hourihan et al., 2016).

claim: Interactions with various cell surface receptors results in NADPH oxidase activation.
source: Importantly, interactions with various cell surface receptors results in NADPH oxidase activation. These include not only receptors involved in immunity signaling but also growth factor receptors (Lambeth and Neish, 2014), with the best-described paradigm being the dependence of EGFR signaling on ROS that are produced by NADPH oxidase in response to EGF binding (Truong and Carroll, 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Lambeth and Neish, 2014; Truong and Carroll, 2012).

claim: All NADPH oxidase signaling events have the potential to impact upon SKN-1/Nrf, and potentially other ROS-responsive mechanisms that influence longevity.
source: Our results suggest that all of these signaling events have the potential to impact upon SKN-1/Nrf, and potentially other ROS-responsive mechanisms that influence longevity.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings that NADPH oxidase ROS activate SKN-1.

claim: NSY-1 and its mammalian homolog ASK-1 are each regulated for activation through cysteine oxidation.
source: Interestingly, NSY-1 and its mammalian homolog ASK-1 are each regulated for activation through cysteine oxidation for activation (Nadeau et al., 2007; Hourihan et al., 2016), suggesting that this kinase may respond directly to BLI-3-generated ROS.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Nadeau et al., 2007; Hourihan et al., 2016).

claim: NSY-1/ASK-1 may respond directly to BLI-3-generated ROS.
source: Interestingly, NSY-1 and its mammalian homolog ASK-1 are each regulated for activation through cysteine oxidation for activation (Nadeau et al., 2007; Hourihan et al., 2016), suggesting that this kinase may respond directly to BLI-3-generated ROS.
evidence: This is speculated based on the known redox regulation of NSY-1/ASK-1.

claim: Signaling from NADPH oxidases has been shown to activate Nrf2-mediated transcription in mammals.
source: Furthermore, signaling from NADPH oxidases has been shown to activate Nrf2-mediated transcription in mammals (Sekhar et al., 2003; Hecker etal., 2014; Brewer et al., 2011; Segal et al., 2010; Schröder et al., 2012; Nlandu Khodo et al., 2012; Hourihan et al., 2016); and RhoA GTPase activity has been linked to NADPH oxidase activation and p38 MAPK signaling (Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: RhoA GTPase activity has been linked to NADPH oxidase activation and p38 MAPK signaling.
source: Furthermore, signaling from NADPH oxidases has been shown to activate Nrf2-mediated transcription in mammals (Sekhar et al., 2003; Hecker etal., 2014; Brewer et al., 2011; Segal et al., 2010; Schröder et al., 2012; Nlandu Khodo et al., 2012; Hourihan et al., 2016); and RhoA GTPase activity has been linked to NADPH oxidase activation and p38 MAPK signaling (Kim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Kim et al., 2005).

claim: Inducing endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in HUVEC cultures leads to active RhoA translocation to the ER membrane, resulting in Nox4-dependent ROS generation at this location.
source: Interestingly, inducing endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in HUVEC cultures leads to active RhoA translocation to the ER membrane, resulting in Nox4-dependent ROS generation at this location (Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Wu et al., 2010).

claim: There is possible conservation of an overall signaling pathway through which mechanisms controlled by MEMO and RhoA activate NADPH oxidase-mediated ROS signaling to act on p38 MAPK and SKN-1/Nrf.
source: Taken together, these findings show a possible conservation of an overall signaling pathway through which mechanisms controlled by MEMO and RhoA activate NADPH oxidase-mediated ROS signaling to act on p38 MAPK and SKN-1/Nrf.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of the C. elegans findings with mammalian literature.

claim: Breast cancer cells that lack Memo1 fail to migrate upon stimulation with growth factors.
source: Breast cancer cells that lack Memo1 fail to migrate upon stimulation with growth factors (Marone et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Marone et al., 2004).

claim: Memo1 is required for the localization of GTP-bound RhoA at the plasma membrane.
source: Moreover, it was shown that Memo1 is required for the localization of GTP-bound RhoA at the plasma membrane (Zaoui et al., 2008), an essential step in the process of cell migration.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Zaoui et al., 2008).

claim: Forcing RhoA to be constitutively membrane-bound rescued the migration phenotype of cells lacking Memo1.
source: Forcing RhoA to be constitutively membrane-bound rescued the migration phenotype of cells lacking Memo1 (Zaoui et al., 2008), suggesting a conserved and biologically relevant interaction between Memo1 and RhoA.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Zaoui et al., 2008).

claim: There is a conserved and biologically relevant interaction between Memo1 and RhoA.
source: Forcing RhoA to be constitutively membrane-bound rescued the migration phenotype of cells lacking Memo1 (Zaoui et al., 2008), suggesting a conserved and biologically relevant interaction between Memo1 and RhoA.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment and conservation between species.

claim: Adult-specific overexpression of RHO-1(G14V) causes lethality within 2-4 days.
source: Unfortunately, overexpression of the constitutively active RHO-1(G14V) GTPase specifically during adulthood causes lethality within 2-4 days (data not shown; [McMullan and Nurrish, 2011]).
evidence: This is stated based on unpublished data and cited literature (McMullan and Nurrish, 2011).

claim: The activity of NADPH oxidase has been shown to be essential during cell migration.
source: The activity of NADPH oxidase has been shown to be essential during cell migration (Stanley et al., 2014; Hurd et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Stanley et al., 2014; Hurd et al., 2012).

claim: Memo1 has been linked to NADPH oxidase activity in breast cancer cells.
source: Interestingly, Memo1 has been linked to NADPH oxidase activity in breast cancer cells (MacDonald et al., 2014), however the exact mechanism underlying these results, as well as a role for RhoA, has not been established and is likely to be context-dependent.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (MacDonald et al., 2014).

claim: Memo1 is a highly conserved protein with homologues found in bacteria through vertebrates.
source: Memo1 is a highly conserved protein with homologues found in bacteria through vertebrates (Schlatter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Schlatter et al., 2012).

claim: The most conserved portion of Memo1 is the domain that has three conserved histidine residues.
source: The most conserved portion of Memo1 is the domain that has three conserved histidine residues. These three histidines, which are present in the C. elegans protein, are required for copper binding, and for Memo1's copper-reducing activity in breast cancer cells (MacDonald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (MacDonald et al., 2014).

claim: Three conserved histidines in Memo1 are required for copper binding and for Memo1's copper-reducing activity in breast cancer cells.
source: The most conserved portion of Memo1 is the domain that has three conserved histidine residues. These three histidines, which are present in the C. elegans protein, are required for copper binding, and for Memo1's copper-reducing activity in breast cancer cells (MacDonald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (MacDonald et al., 2014).

claim: MEMO-1 might sense ROS through its metal-binding domain, which might provide a feedback mechanism that regulates the ROS-generating pathway.
source: One speculative but exciting possibility for a future study would be to investigate whether MEMO-1 might sense ROS through this metal-binding domain, and whether this might provide a feedback mechanism that regulates this ROS-generating pathway.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation for future investigation.

claim: In mice, loss of NADPH oxidase activity accelerated aging.
source: In mice, loss of NADPH oxidase activity accelerated aging (Chen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Chen et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2011).

claim: Chronic ROS generation by NADPH oxidase has been suggested to promote age-dependent diseases.
source: By contrast, chronic ROS generation by NADPH oxidase has been suggested to promote age-dependent diseases (Krause, 2007), showing that NADPH oxidase and the generated ROS need to be tightly regulated.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Krause, 2007).

claim: Transient or low NADPH oxidase-generated ROS act as a signal to re-establish homeostasis during aging.
source: Our data reveal that transient or low NADPH oxidase-generated ROS act as a signal to re-establish homeostasis during aging, and imply that signals that affect NADPH oxidase activity can also influence longevity.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the combined findings of the study.

claim: Signals that affect NADPH oxidase activity can influence longevity.
source: Our data reveal that transient or low NADPH oxidase-generated ROS act as a signal to re-establish homeostasis during aging, and imply that signals that affect NADPH oxidase activity can also influence longevity.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the findings that modulating NADPH oxidase activity affects lifespan.

claim: NADPH oxidase activity is inducible and controllable, suggesting a novel target for therapeutics to promote healthy aging.
source: An exciting aspect of our findings is that NADPH oxidase activity is inducible and controllable, suggesting a novel target for therapeutics to promote healthy aging.
evidence: This is speculation about therapeutic implications based on the study findings.

claim: Chronic exposure to ROS leads to cellular damage and age-associated diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and chronic inflammation.
source: Chronic exposure to ROS leads to cellular damage and age-associated diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, cancer, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and chronic inflammation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Low or acute ROS exposure mobilizes protective mechanisms and increases lifespan in S. cerevisiae, D. melanogaster, C. elegans, and rodents.
source: By contrast, low or acute ROS exposure mobilizes protective mechanisms and increases lifespan in S. cerevisiae (Pan et al., 2011; Mesquita et al., 2010; Schroeder et al., 2013), D. melanogaster (Albrecht et al., 2011), C. elegans (Schulz et al., 2007; Doonan et al., 2008; Yang and Hekimi, 2010; Schmeisser et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010), and rodents (Lapointe and Hekimi, 2008; Liu et al., 2005), and has been associated with health benefits in humans (Ristow et al., 2009, 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on multiple cited studies across different organisms.

claim: Low or acute ROS exposure has been associated with health benefits in humans.
source: By contrast, low or acute ROS exposure mobilizes protective mechanisms and increases lifespan in S. cerevisiae (Pan et al., 2011; Mesquita et al., 2010; Schroeder et al., 2013), D. melanogaster (Albrecht et al., 2011), C. elegans (Schulz et al., 2007; Doonan et al., 2008; Yang and Hekimi, 2010; Schmeisser et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010), and rodents (Lapointe and Hekimi, 2008; Liu et al., 2005), and has been associated with health benefits in humans (Ristow et al., 2009, 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Ristow et al., 2009, 2014).

claim: Hormesis is defined as the induction of protective mechanisms under exposure to low doses of stressful agents, which at higher or prolonged exposures are harmful.
source: Hormesis is defined as the induction of protective mechanisms under exposure to low doses of stressful agents, which at higher or prolonged exposures are harmful.
evidence: This is a definition of hormesis provided in the text.

claim: Ninety percent of cellular ROS arise as a by-product of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Ninety percent of cellular ROS arise as a by-product of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (Halliwell and Gutteridge, 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Halliwell and Gutteridge, 2007).

claim: Moderate mitochondrial dysfunction leads to elevation of mitochondrial-derived ROS, activating protective mechanisms (mitohormesis) and promoting longevity.
source: Moderate mitochondrial dysfunction leads to elevation of mitochondrial-derived ROS, activating protective mechanisms (mitohormesis) and promoting longevity (Ristow and Schmeisser, 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Ristow and Schmeisser, 2014).

claim: Several longevity interventions, such as dietary restriction or reduced insulin/IGF-1 signaling, are associated with an increase in mitochondrial ROS levels, which acts as a retrograde signal to increase lifespan.
source: Several longevity interventions, such as dietary restriction or reduced insulin/IGF-1 signaling, are associated with an increase in mitochondrial ROS levels, which acts as a retrograde signal to increase lifespan (Schulz et al., 2007; Weimer et al., 2014; Zarse et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Schulz et al., 2007; Weimer et al., 2014; Zarse et al., 2012).

claim: ROS promote receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling by oxidizing a cysteine residue in protein-tyrosine phosphatase 1 (PTP1), thereby transiently inactivating its phosphatase activity.
source: For instance, ROS promote receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling by oxidizing a cysteine residue in protein-tyrosine phosphatase 1 (PTP1), thereby transiently inactivating its phosphatase activity (Salmeen et al., 2003; Goldstein et al., 2005) and potentiating the activity of its partner RTK.
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Salmeen et al., 2003; Goldstein et al., 2005).

claim: Localized ROS that act as signals do so at short range (~5–20 µm) with a half-life of ~1 ms.
source: Localized ROS that act as signals do so at short range (~5–20 µm; [Winterbourn, 2008]) with a half-life of ~1 ms (D'Autréaux and Toledano, 2007), in part due to high intracellular concentration of the antioxidant glutathione (1–10 mM; [Meister, 1988]), which keeps the cytosol in a reduced environment (Gilbert, 1990; Romero-Aristizabal et al., 2014; Lambeth and Neish, 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature.

claim: Pools of localized ROS must be rapidly generated for redox signaling to occur.
source: Hence, pools of localized ROS must be rapidly generated for redox signaling to occur.
evidence: This is inferred from the short half-life and range of ROS signals.

claim: Cells have membrane-associated enzymes that generate ROS, using nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) as an electron donor to produce a local ROS micro-environment.
source: In addition to ROS derived as a by-product of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, cells have membrane-associated enzymes that generate ROS, using nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) as an electron donor to produce a local ROS micro-environment (Bedard and Krause, 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Bedard and Krause, 2007).

claim: NADPH oxidases form complexes with subunits required for their stability and activation.
source: In general, NADPH oxidases form complexes with subunits required for their stability and activation (Bedard and Krause, 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Bedard and Krause, 2007).

claim: Upon stimulation of cell surface receptors, GTP-bound Rho-GTPase family members and p21-activated kinase-1 (PAK1) must be recruited to the NADPH oxidase complex to generate ROS.
source: For instance, upon stimulation of cell surface receptors, guanosine-trisphospate (GTP) bound Rho-guanosine-triphosphatase (GTPase) family members and p21-activated kinase-1 (PAK1) must be recruited to the NADPH oxidase complex to generate ROS (Hurd et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Hurd et al., 2012).

claim: Mammals have seven NADPH oxidase family members.
source: Mammals have seven NADPH oxidase family members, which have been found in almost every tissue and are localized at cellular membranes and within intracellular compartments, such as endosomes and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Bedard and Krause, 2007; Krause, 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Bedard and Krause, 2007; Krause, 2007).

claim: Mammalian NADPH oxidases have been implicated in a wide range of normal physiological functions, as well as in diseases that include cancer.
source: Mammalian NADPH oxidases have been implicated in a wide range of normal physiological functions, (Bedard and Krause, 2007; Krause, 2007), as well as in diseases that include cancer (Truong and Carroll, 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Bedard and Krause, 2007; Krause, 2007; Truong and Carroll, 2012).

claim: NADPH oxidase-generated ROS act as a second messenger to regulate migration of metastasis-committed-cancer cells and as a chemoattractant for immune cells during wound healing.
source: NADPH oxidase-generated ROS have been shown to act as a second messenger to regulate migration of metastasis-committed-cancer cells and as a chemoattractant for immune cells during wound healing (Stanley et al., 2014; Hurd et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Stanley et al., 2014; Hurd et al., 2012).

claim: Mediator of ErbB2 driven cell motility (Memo1) plays an important role in migration of breast cancer cells and is needed for robust metastatic dissemination from primary tumors to lungs.
source: Mediator of ErbB2 driven cell motility (Memo1) has been shown to play an important role in migration of breast cancer cells and is needed for robust metastatic dissemination from primary tumors to lungs (Marone et al., 2004; MacDonald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Marone et al., 2004; MacDonald et al., 2014).

claim: During the migratory process Memo1 interacts with Rho GTPase to dynamically reorganize actin and microtubule fibers.
source: During the migratory process Memo1 interacts with Rho GTPase to dynamically reorganize actin and microtubule fibers (Zaoui et al., 2008), and has also been linked to NADPH oxidase activity in breast cancer cells (MacDonald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on cited literature (Zaoui et al., 2008).
